A big bet on Argentine soybeans

Molinos Agro and ACA are putting more than US$500 million into a new soybean crushing plant in Timbues, Santa Fe. Timbues is on the Parana River, a key route for shipping grain.

Molinos Agro will own 65% of the project. ACA, a group of Argentine farm cooperatives, will own the other 35%.

The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans each day. That is about 5 million tons a year, which would make it one of the biggest crush plants in the country.

This is the first major new soy crushing investment in twelve years. It was announced on 8 July 2026, and building will take about three years.

The plant will turn soybeans into meal and oil for world markets inside Argentina. This adds value at home instead of shipping raw beans.

Why export taxes matter here

The project needs a planned cut in export taxes, called retenciones or DEX. The Argentine government will reduce these taxes slowly, starting in January 2027.

Under this plan, soybean export taxes drop from 24% to 21% by the end of 2027. By December 2028, they would go down further to 15%.

Lower export taxes make it cheaper to sell soybean products abroad. That helps profits for a new crush plant, so the investment depends on this tax schedule.

The gap between soy and maize export taxes matters. Consultant Javier Preciado Patino, writing on 14 August 2026, says it is 15.5 points now.

It will fall to 13.5 points in 2027. By late 2028, it will be about 9.5 points.

The Bolsa de Comercio de Rosario, an exchange in the grain city of Rosario, tracks total tax payments. It says the six main agricultural chains will pay US$4,613 million in export taxes in 2026.

That is down from US$4,665 million in 2025, a fall of about 1%.

For 2026, the breakdown is: soybeans US$3,275 million, maize US$754 million, wheat US$324 million, sunflower US$158 million, barley US$79 million, and sorghum US$22 million.

The plant will cost more than US$500 million. That is a large capital outlay for Argentina’s agribusiness sector.

What the tax schedule means for the plant

The plant was announced in July 2026, but the tax changes are new. The schedule makes the project work by improving profit margins over the next few years.

As soybean export taxes drop, it becomes more attractive to crush beans in Argentina. The soy-versus-maize gap is key because it affects which crops farmers plant and how much they process.

The tax plan is not a signed decree yet. It depends on future policy decisions and could change.

If the schedule slips, the plant’s economics could change too. Watch the January 2027 start date, because that is when the bet starts to pay off.

The numbers behind the investment

The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans each day, or about 5 million tons per year. That makes it one of the biggest crushing plants in the country.

This project is a bet on policy, not just on production. It expects Argentina to keep more soybeans at home for processing, instead of sending them out raw.

US Department of Agriculture forecasts for Argentina have not changed. The investment is based on local policy shifts, not US reports.

Why this matters for Latin America investors

For people invested in Argentine farming, this plant shows trust in the country’s export future. It also shows how tax cuts and other policy changes can push large investments.

Soybeans bring in billions of dollars in export income every year. A new crushing plant could change where value is added, keeping more of it in Argentina.

Workers and local suppliers in Santa Fe may gain new jobs and demand. Ports near Timbues will likely handle more soybean meal and oil exports.

This is the first big soy crushing investment in twelve years. That marks a renewed sense of confidence in Argentine soybeans.

World.title: Chile’s Falabella Founders Keep Selling Down Their Stake

The Cuneo family sold a 1% block on 13 August, while LarrainVial paused new contributions to a fund and Mallplaza revived a shopping centre project.

Chilean retailer Falabella’s founding families have sold 2.49% of the company during 2026. The latest sale was a 1% block by the Cuneo family on 13 August.

Cuneo family sells 1% block

The Cuneo family sold 25 million Falabella shares on 13 August 2026. That is 1% of the retail company.

Bethia, tied to the Heller Solari family, sold two tranches. The first was 12.5 million shares for CLP 79,375 million on 20 January.

The second was 12.5 million shares for CLP 81,375 million on 23 January.

Paola Cuneo sold through Inversiones Santa Victoria SpA. Giorgianna Cuneo sold through Inversiones Cinque Terre SpA.

Each sold 12.5 million shares at an average price of CLP 6,300.20 each. The total value was CLP 157,504 million, about US$172.7 million.

The broker LarrainVial executed the block trade at about 10:30. After the sale, the Cuneo family’s combined holding fell to 8.24%, down from about 9.24%.

Founding families reduce stakes through 2026

The Cuneo sale is part of a wider trend. The founding families have sold 2.49% of Falabella in 2026.

These sales total CLP 401,549 million, about US$439 million, based on filings with Chile’s securities regulator, the CMF.

Mis Inversiones SpA, linked to the Del Rio Goudie family, sold 10 million shares, 0.39%, for CLP 65,100 million on 23 January. DT D y D, linked to Juan Pablo del Rio, sold 3 million shares, 0.12%, for CLP 18,195 million on 19 June.

LarrainVial pauses fund contributions

On 17 August 2026, LarrainVial’s LV Enfoque fund stopped new contributions for a while. The fund had about US$640 million at the end of July.

The manager wants to check if market liquidity levels will stay. Redemptions still work, and there are exceptions for planned savings plans and dividend reinvestment.

This is about the fund’s size and market liquidity, not a problem with the Santiago exchange.

Mallplaza revives Concón project

Separately, Mallplaza restarted a long-paused mall project in Concón. It shared the new design on 17 August 2026.

The project will be an open-air lifestyle centre at Bosques de Montemar. It will cost about US$80 million and have 50,000 square metres of leasable space, with around 200 shops.

The 2012 plan was 60,000 square metres and US$120 million, but it was dropped in 2024. The land has been involved since a purchase in 2011.

Mallplaza has talked with local residents and authorities about the new plan. Building is expected to finish around 2030.

Why this matters for investors

If you own Falabella shares, watch how they are sold. When founding families reduce their shares, it often means they see limited future gains.

The stock closed at CLP 6,180 on 14 August, the last close before Monday. That is the key price point to watch.

For those invested in Chilean retail, the Concón project is positive. It shows Mallplaza is willing to invest in growth after years of delay.

LarrainVial’s role as broker is notable. It handles major block trades, and its fund pause reflects a cautious stance on liquidity.

Who else has been selling

The Cuneo block was not the first sale this year. Bethia, the vehicle of the Heller Solari family, sold two tranches in January.

The first was 12,500,000 shares for CLP$79,375 million (about US$87 million) on 20 January. The second was another 12,500,000 shares for CLP$81,375 million (about US$89 million) on 23 January.

On the same day in January, Mis Inversiones SpA, linked to Del Rio Goudie, sold 10,000,000 shares — 0.39% of the company — for CLP$65,100 million (about US$71 million).

DT D y D, linked to Juan Pablo del Rio, followed in June with 3,000,000 shares, or 0.12%, for CLP$18,195 million (about US$20 million).

What Mallplaza is actually reviving

The Concon project has a long history. Mallplaza bought the land in 2011 and drew up a plan in 2012 for 60,000 square metres at a cost of about US$120 million.

That version was dropped in 2024. What returns now is smaller and open-air.

The new plan is about US$80 million for 50,000 square metres of leasable space and around 200 shops at Bosques de Montemar. It is due to open in 2030.

World.title: Colombia’s State Broadcaster Reviews US$32 Million of Contracts
World.content:
Key Facts Contracts More than 1,051 contracts were signed in the current budget year under the public media system.

More than 1,051 contracts were signed in the current budget year under the public media system. Value The combined value exceeds COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million at current exchange rates).

The combined value exceeds COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million at current exchange rates). Recent Between 6 and 7 August 2026, officials signed 87 contracts worth about COP 4,000 million (about US$1.3 million).

Between 6 and 7 August 2026, officials signed 87 contracts worth about COP 4,000 million (about US$1.3 million). Review All these contracts will be reviewed as part of a reorganisation announced by the new management of Inravision.

All these contracts will be reviewed as part of a reorganisation announced by the new management of Inravision. Entity Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC, manages the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia.

Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC, manages the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia. Context President Abelardo De la Espriella’s government has moved to restructure public institutions since taking office.

Colombia · Government

New management of Colombia’s public media system will review more than 1,051 contracts worth over COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million).

Colombia’s new public media management will review more than 1,051 contracts signed this year. The total value exceeds COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million). The review is part of a broader push for transparency under President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on 7 August 2026. For anyone who does business with the state, this is a signal: contracts signed under the previous government are now under the microscope.

Colombia’s State Broadcaster Reviews US$32 Million of Contracts. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the contract review covers

On 17 August 2026, a MinTIC statement following an extraordinary board meeting on 15 August disclosed the contract numbers. The statement came from the new administration of the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia, which operates as Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC.

The statement said the contracts were signed in the current budget year. The total value is more than COP 100,000 million, which equals about US$32 million.

Between 6 and 7 August 2026, 87 contracts were signed for approximately COP 4,000 million. That is about US$1.3 million.

All of these processes will be subject to review as part of the reorganisation announced by the new management of Inravision. The review aims to check how the contracts were awarded.

The reorganisation began on 7 August, right after the news programming strand, the franja informativa, ended on 6 August.

Understanding the institutional names

The organisation formerly called RTVC Sistema de Medios Publicos is now Inravision Sistema de Medios Publicos. RTVC announced in April 2026 that it was taking back its historic name.

Write it as ‘Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC’.

The new gerente — general manager — is Angela Maria Mora Soto, a lawyer appointed by the government of Abelardo De la Espriella. She replaces Hollman Morris.

The ICT minister is Alexandra Falla.

Do not assume these 1,051 contracts belong solely to RTVC. The reporting groups them under the public media system umbrella.

This difference matters for investors and professionals who follow government contracts. The legal entity in charge of each contract can change.

Why the review matters now

President Abelardo De la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026.

The contract review is part of a wider reorganisation of public media. This may lead to new buying rules or the ending of some contracts.

For businesses that work with public broadcasters, this review creates uncertainty. Existing contracts may be delayed or renegotiated.

The review also shows how the new administration wants to spend public money. They will look closely at contracts signed by the previous government.

What happens next

The new management has not said when the review will finish. They have said all processes will be checked during the restructuring.

No contracts have been cancelled or suspended so far. The review is still in its early stages.

Watch for news from Inravision about findings or changes. The government may also release new rules for contracts.

For now, this is a review, not a cancellation. Contract holders should watch for updates and keep their documents ready.

This review is part of a larger effort by the De la Espriella government to change state agencies. The pension reform and diplomatic appointments are also being looked at.

Vilma Velasquez, Colombia’s ambassador to Haiti, is under investigation by the foreign ministry. The issue is about US$500,000 in unexplained transfers, including a cheque from the embassy’s operating account to her personal account.

This was reported on 7 August 2026. She denies the claim, saying 500,000 dollars never came in.

She was already suspended by the Procuraduria in May 2026 for backing Ivan Cepeda in politics.

The Constitutional Court may send the pension reform back to Congress again. This would be the second time.

The plans for savers and for moving funds to Colpensiones are still being discussed.

The total amount is about COP 25 billones, which is close to 25 trillion Colombian pesos. That is about US$8 billion.

These actions share a common idea: the new government is taking more control over institutions and contracts. Investors should expect more reviews and possible changes in policy.

Broader context for investors

Vilma Velasquez, Colombia’s ambassador to Haiti, is under investigation by the foreign ministry over about US$500,000 in unjustified transfers, including a cheque from the embassy’s operating account to her personal account. This came out on 7 August 2026. She denies it, saying 500,000 dollars never came in. She had already been suspended by the Procuraduria in May 2026 for political participation, for backing Ivan Cepeda.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many contracts are under review? More than 1,051 contracts signed in the current budget year are under review. They belong to the public media system managed by Inravision. What is the total value of the contracts? The total value exceeds COP 100,000 million, which is about US$32 million. An additional 87 contracts signed in early August are worth about COP 4,000 million (US$1.3 million). Are these contracts being cancelled? No. They are under review as part of a reorganisation. No cancellations have been announced so far. Which entity signed these contracts? The reporting refers to the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia and Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC. The figures cover the public media system.

World.title: A Week On, Colombia’s Quake Toll Is Still Moving
World.content:
Colombia · Disaster

Key Facts The toll As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued.

As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued. The damage The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments.

The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments. The reach The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads.

The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads. Numbers move both ways The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed.

The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed. A private cheque David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction.

David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction. The politics A censure motion against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán was announced on 17 August. This happened because of photographs of him on the beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

Seven days after a magnitude 7.4 quake hit Chocó, the official count is still being revised in both directions — and the politics has arrived.

If you have been trying to follow Colombia’s earthquake from abroad, the hardest part is that the numbers keep changing. A week after the magnitude 7.4 quake struck on 10 August, centred five kilometres south of San José del Palmar in Chocó, the official toll has gone up and then back down. Here is where it actually stood at the last full count, and what has happened around it since.

A Week On, Colombia’s Quake Toll Is Still Moving. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where the count stands

The national disaster agency, UNGRD, gives updates from time to time, not live numbers. Its last full count, at 18:30 on 16 August, showed 287 dead and 4,147 injured.

Another 194 people are still missing. Also, 355 have been pulled out alive.

Watch these two numbers because the gap between them shows where the toll will change next. The damage is huge for a country this size.

26,392 homes were destroyed. 127,608 were damaged, and 197 buildings fell.

Damage hit 472 municipalities across 15 departments. Public buildings also suffered: 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads were affected.

On 15 August, the official figure was 294. On 16 August, it was 287.

A falling toll can look scary if you have not seen it before, so here is why. In the first days after a disaster, the same person may be counted more than once.

For example, one count may come from a town, another from a hospital, and another from a rescue team. As names get confirmed, duplicate counts are removed.

For anyone watching from far away, write down the time and date for every number you see. A figure without a date is not very useful this week.

This is the mistake most news reports make. On 12 August, the governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi, said the search and rescue phase was over in her area.

She said they were no longer looking for people under the rubble.

Why the death toll went down

The search is over in Chocó, not nationally

That rule applies only to Chocó. The national emergency is still active, because 194 people remain missing.

So reports that Colombia has stopped searching are only partly correct. Chocó has moved to rebuilding, but other areas have not.

Money, tolls and a minister at the beach

David Vélez, founder and leader of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million — about US$32 million — for reconstruction. He confirmed this himself after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it.

The road agency ANI, led by president Ricardo Ayerbe, has removed tolls, but less widely than news suggests. The waiver covers trucks with heavy machines, emergency gear, and aid supplies, on specific roads only.

Those roads are Buga–Buenaventura, Malla Vial del Valle, Armenia–Pereira–Manizales, Tercer Carril Bogotá–Girardot, and Girardot–Ibagué–Cajamarca. Fines for overloaded trucks are paused, so aid vehicles are not penalised.

Private car drivers still pay.

Politics has entered too. On 17 August, a censure motion was announced against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán, due to photos of him at a beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

It is announced, but not yet voted on.

What this means if you live in or invest in the region

Housing will shape the coming two years. With 26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, this becomes a rebuilding and money story long after rescue work ends.

The roads on ANI’s list are the same ones used for cargo between Buenaventura, Colombia’s main Pacific port, and the inland areas. Businesses moving goods through that port should check ANI notices, not general headlines.

The Vélez donation matters for another reason. US$32 million from one private person is a big part of the early rebuilding costs.

This amount sets a new level for other big Colombian companies to compare with.

The censure motion shows how fast disaster aid turns into politics in this country. If you have projects waiting for housing-ministry decisions, this is a delay risk you should plan for.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in Colombia’s earthquake? The national disaster agency UNGRD recorded 287 deaths in its cut at 18:30 on 16 August 2026, with 4,147 injured and 194 people still missing. The figure moves between cuts, so always check the date attached to it. Why did the death toll go down? It was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Early counts often double-record the same victim through different channels, and duplicates are removed as identities are confirmed. Has the search for survivors ended? In Chocó, yes — the governor declared the search and rescue phase over on 12 August. Nationally it remains open, with 194 people still unaccounted for. Are Colombia’s toll roads free after the earthquake? Only for specific vehicles. ANI has exempted vehicles carrying heavy machinery, emergency equipment and humanitarian aid on a defined list of corridors, and suspended overload fines. Private cars still pay.

World.title: Peru’s Mining Boom: Investment Up 42.7%, Not 74%
World.content:
Peru · Mining

Key Facts Investment rise Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina.

Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina. The 74% myth A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total.

A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total. Top spenders Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%).

Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). Company profits MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash.

MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash. Quellaveco shines Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier. Copper giant Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m).

Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m). Weak spot Exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million, even as investment boomed.

The real story: Peru’s mining investment hit US$3.3 billion in H1 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. That 74% figure? It’s a Mexican miner’s revenue.

If you’ve seen headlines about Peru’s mining sector surging 74%, you might be forgiven for thinking the country is swimming in cash. But the actual official figure is different: mining investment rose 42.7% to US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) via state news agency Andina. The 74% bump belongs to Fresnillo, a Mexico-only miner—not Peru. Let’s clear up the confusion so you know what’s really happening on the ground.

An open-pit operation in the Peruvian Andes. Mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The real numbers from MINEM

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) says mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. That is 42.7% more than the US$2.3152 billion from the same time last year.

This is the official total for the whole mining sector. It shows steady growth, but not the 74% jump that some headlines mention.

MINEM lists the top investors as Southern Peru, Shougang Hierro Peru, Las Bambas, Antamina, Buenaventura, and Cerro Verde. Southern Peru alone spent US$432.7 million, which is 101.1% above a year ago.

Exploration spending is the weak part. It rose only 1.3%, reaching US$336.4 million.

Investment is strong, but finding new mineral deposits is slow. For comparison, US$3.304 billion equals about 11.1 billion soles, using the rate of 3.3647 soles per US dollar.

This healthy number shows mining firms are confident and spending on projects. That is important because Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer.

The 74% figure is real, but it does not apply to Peru. It comes from Fresnillo, a mining company based in Mexico, whose first-half 2026 revenue rose 74.7% to US$3.38 billion.

Fresnillo also reported a net profit of US$1.46 billion, up 213%. But it has no mines in Peru—its operations are at Saucito, Herradura, Juanicipio, Fresnillo, Cienega, and San Julian.

That 74% figure does not reflect Peru’s mining health. If you see such claims, check the source carefully.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru earned US$2.161 billion in revenue. That is up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025, a 41.8% increase.

Higher copper prices and output helped the rise. Production was slightly lower, but the result still improved.

The official Peruvian number is the 42.7% investment rise. Trust that one instead.

Why does this matter? Investment shows what companies plan for the future.

Profits can change quickly, but spending signals long-term confidence.

The confusion likely comes from mixing company results with sector data. For example, MMG’s profit jumped, but that is just one firm, not all miners.

Fresnillo’s revenue growth is big, but it belongs to a different country. Peru-linked miners still had a strong first half, even if the 74% headline is wrong.

MMG, which runs the Las Bambas copper mine in Peru, reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%. Profit for equity holders was US$897.2 million.

Some say 141% growth, but that number is for cash, not earnings. Las Bambas drove the result, and MMG called it its best financial performance in over ten years.

Southern Copper, which operates major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%. Its second quarter alone brought in US$4,289.0 million.

Where the 74% figure really comes from

Company-level wins that tell the real story

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru generated US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025. That’s a 41.8% increase, driven by higher copper prices and production—even though output was slightly lower. Southern Copper, which runs major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%; the second quarter alone was US$4,289.0 million.

Buenaventura, a Peruvian miner, saw net income attributable of US$514.0 million on H1 revenue of US$1,153.6 million, both clearly higher than the same period in 2025. Nexa Resources’ Peru subsidiary, Nexa Resources Peru S.A.A., reported US$669 million in revenue, up 45%—not the group.

The Nexa group’s first-half revenue was US$1,796 million, up 34%.

Why this matters for you

If you’re invested in Latin America, these numbers matter because they show where capital is flowing. Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer, and rising investment means more supply coming online—which could affect global copper prices and your portfolio.

For instance, MMG’s record profit and Southern Copper’s revenue surge are signals that copper demand remains strong.

For expats living in Peru, a mining boom often translates into more jobs, stronger local economies in mining regions, and a firmer sol. The currency has been stable, with the exchange rate around 3.36 soles per US dollar.

Mining investment also supports infrastructure and local businesses, from equipment suppliers to service providers.

But don’t get caught up in the hype. The 74% figure is a classic example of a number being taken out of context. Stick to the official MINEM data, and you’ll have a clearer picture of what’s actually happening. And if you’re watching specific stocks, remember that company-level results can vary widely—so look at each miner’s own numbers, not just the sector headline. Also, note that Peru’s energy and mines minister is Guillermo Shinno Huamani, sworn in in late July 2026 under President Keiko Fujimori—his office is the source for the official investment data.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the official figure for Peru’s mining investment in H1 2026? Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported mining investment of US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. Where does the 74% figure come from? The 74% figure is actually Fresnillo’s revenue growth—up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion. Fresnillo is a Mexico-only miner, not a Peru-specific metric. Which companies led mining investment in Peru? According to MINEM, the top investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). How did Peru-linked miners perform in H1 2026? MMG’s Las Bambas contributed to a US$1,366.0 million profit after tax, up 89%. Anglo American’s Quellaveco saw US$2.161 billion in revenue. Southern Copper reported first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%.

World.title: Mexico’s Military Service Draw: Who the 2026 Lottery Covers
World.content:
Mexico · Explainer

Key Facts Lottery date: The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published.

The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published. Who is drawn: The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby). 18–39 range: That age bracket exists only because the law’s obligations run to 31 December of the year a man turns 40. ‘Remisos’ — men who never registered — can be anywhere in that range. It’s not a new conscription band.

It’s not a new conscription band. Registration windows: The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries in the second half of the year a man turns 18. The 2026 convocatoria opens the municipal window from 2 January to 15 October 2026.

The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries in the second half of the year a man turns 18. The 2026 convocatoria opens the municipal window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. Cartilla liberation: The cartilla (military ID card) is liberated in December 2026. Those assigned ‘encuadrado’ attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The cartilla (military ID card) is liberated in December 2026. Those assigned ‘encuadrado’ attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027. Voluntary for women: Women have been able to take part voluntarily since 2000 and are not subject to encuadramiento.

Women have been able to take part voluntarily since 2000 and are not subject to encuadramiento. Beyond the law: Claims that everyone aged 18 to 39 will be integrated into the Army if drawn go beyond what the law and SEDENA explicitly state. Treat them with caution.

The November draft lottery has a clear target group — and it isn’t everyone aged 18 to 39.

If you’ve seen posts claiming Mexico is about to draft everyone aged 18 to 39 into the Army, take a breath. Nothing changed this month. The claim doing the rounds is recycled coverage of SEDENA’s January 2026 convocatoria — the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

Mexico’s military service draw is held in November. No new rule was announced in August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the lottery actually is

SMN is Mexico’s required military service. Under the Ley del Servicio Militar, ‘service of arms’ is a duty for Mexican citizens by birth or naturalization.

The lottery decides if men are ‘encuadrado’ — meaning they must train. Or they are ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

For 2026, the group is ‘Clase 2008’ — men born in 2008 who turn 18 this year. SEDENA (Mexico’s defense ministry) said the lottery for this group will be in November 2026.

Those picked for encuadrado attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The 18-to-39 age number online is true, but it doesn’t mean what viral posts suggest. It refers to ‘remisos’ — men who missed their SMN paperwork on time.

These men still must fix their status. A remiso must regularize their status to get their military card.

They remain obligated until December 31 of the year they turn 40. So the age range can be 18 to 39.

The law was first published in 1940. Its latest update was on May 18, 2022.

The process has five steps: registration (alistamiento), lottery (sorteo), recruitment (reclutamiento), training (adiestramiento), and freeing your military card (liberación).

So the 18-to-39 window is about fixing missed paperwork, not a new draft for all up to middle age. The main group is still men turning 18 in 2026.

For Mexican men, the SMN is an ‘obligación ineludible’ (unavoidable duty), per SEDENA communications. If you’re a man turning 18 in 2026, registration is a legal duty, not a choice.

If chosen encuadrado, attending the 13 Saturday sessions is required. Missing them could mean legal trouble, with up to one year in prison as the law mentions.

The 18-to-39 age range, explained

What’s compulsory, and for whom

For women, the rules are different. Participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento.

This has been the case since 2000.

What’s actually new for 2026

The basic structure of the SMN hasn’t changed. There’s no new SEDENA notice and nothing in the official gazette for August 2026.

The claim doing the rounds is the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

The 2026 convocatoria, which dates to January, opens the municipal registration window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries for the second half of the year a man turns 18.

This is the same annual process. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ — meaning you serve — and a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’.

Cartilla liberation is in December 2026.

Why this matters for you

If you’re a Mexican man who never completed your SMN paperwork, the clock is ticking. The remiso window is real, and the November 2026 lottery for Clase 2008 is the one that applies to you most directly if you’re in that class.

But even if you’re older, you still need to regularize to get your cartilla before turning 40.

For expats and investors, the practical takeaway is simpler: there’s no mass mobilization coming. The SMN is a long-standing administrative process, and the 18-to-39 scare is a misreading of the remiso rule.

Your neighbor with a desk job isn’t about to be drafted.

If you have employees or family members facing this, the real deadline is paper-based: register, get your cartilla, and you’re done. The lottery is a formality for most.

Nothing in the sources suggests a shift that would affect labor markets, investment, or day-to-day life beyond the usual paperwork. The only people who need to act are those who’ve fallen behind on their SMN obligations — and they should treat this as a reminder to catch up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is everyone aged 18 to 39 being drafted into the Mexican Army? No. The 18-to-39 range refers to ’remisos’ — men who missed registering for the SMN when they were due and must regularize their status to get their cartilla. The main conscription class for 2026 is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year. Claims about a mass draft of everyone up to 39 go beyond what the law and SEDENA state. When is the 2026 military service lottery? For Clase 2008, SEDENA officially informed that the lottery will be held in November 2026. The exact day hasn’t been published. Is military service compulsory for women in Mexico? No. Women’s participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento. This has been the case since 2000. What happens if I miss the registration deadline? You become a ’remiso’ — a man who didn’t complete SMN paperwork when due. You must regularize your status to obtain your cartilla, and you remain under obligation until December 31 of the year you turn 40. Legal consequences, including up to one year of prison by court order, are referenced under the law, though sources don’t clarify if this is newly enforced.

World.title: Guanacaste Airport Outpaces Costa Rica’s Main Airport
World.content:
Costa Rica welcomed more than 2 million international tourists during the first seven months of 2026, but the clearest sign of change was not simply how many people arrived. It was where they chose to land. Guanacaste Airport in Liberia recorded the strongest airport growth, reinforcing its role as the main gateway to Costa Rica’s northern Pacific beaches.

For those heading to Tamarindo, Playas del Coco, the Papagayo Peninsula or other parts of the Nicoya Peninsula, flying into Liberia can eliminate the need to cross the Central Valley and then make the long drive west. The airport’s expanding network of direct flights is making that option available to more visitors.

A total of 698,079 international tourists entered Costa Rica through the Guanacaste airport between January and July, an increase of 13.3% from the same period in 2025. In July alone, the airport received 89,947 visitors, up 12.6%. Juan Santamaría International Airport remained Costa Rica’s busiest entry point, welcoming 1,154,732 international tourists during the seven-month period. Arrivals at the Alajuela airport grew by 3.6%, including 158,076 visitors in July.

Together, the two airports accounted for most of the 2,001,660 international tourists who visited Costa Rica from January through July. The overall number was 6.4% higher than during the same period last year. Air travel continued to power the tourism industry, accounting for 1,853,430 arrivals and growing by 7%. Another 142,780 visitors entered by land or water, although arrivals through those routes declined by 1.7%.

The figures also reveal a gradual shift in where Costa Rica’s visitors are coming from. The United States remained the largest tourism market by a wide margin, sending 1,142,234 visitors during the first seven months of the year. Americans accounted for 57% of all international arrivals, but growth from the United States was almost flat at 0.4%.

That makes the performance of other international markets increasingly important. Canada recorded one of the strongest increases, with 220,691 Canadian tourists arriving between January and July, up 24.4%. Costa Rica also received 315,340 visitors from Europe, an increase of 8.4%.

Arrivals grew from North America, South America, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, the Caribbean and the Middle East. Visitor numbers from Central America and Africa declined. The July results also brought some relief after tourism arrivals slipped in June. For hotels, vacation rentals, restaurants, transportation providers and tour companies, continued growth heading into the year-end high season would be welcome.

Still, the gains are not evenly distributed. Costa Rica’s tourism growth is increasingly being driven by Guanacaste Airport and markets such as Canada and Europe, while the much larger U.S. market remains largely unchanged. More than the two-million-visitor milestone, that changing pattern may be the most important tourism story of 2026.

World.title: Costa Rica Flooding Forces 500 Into Shelters as Pacific Side Runs Dry
World.content:
Two tropical waves crossed Costa Rica in three days, leaving nearly 500 people in emergency shelters, 862 schools closed and the Caribbean coast, the Northern Zone and Turrialba under an orange alert that still stands this afternoon. If you are in any of those areas, plan around the rain this week rather than waiting for it to pass.

What gets lost in the flood footage is that the other half is having its driest stretch of the year. Guanacaste carries no alert at all. Same country, same three days, opposite extremes, and one pattern out in the Pacific Ocean driving both of them.

The rain is not the real problem anymore

Soil in the Caribbean river basins is now between 90% and 100% saturated. In the southern Pacific it is above 85%.That figure matters more than any rainfall total. Saturated ground behaves like a full sponge, so whatever falls next runs straight off the surface into rivers and streets instead of soaking in.

It also means a modest shower can now do what a heavy one did a week ago. Rivers rise faster, hillsides give way more easily, and storm drains in town centers back up within minutes rather than hours.

Two tropical waves, back to back

Tropical wave No. 32 crossed Costa Rica on Saturday and Sunday. No. 33 followed on Monday, arriving while the Intertropical Convergence Zone sat over and trade winds pushed moisture in off the Caribbean Sea. Over the weekend, six-hour rainfall in Cahuita, Limón and Talamanca reached 70 to 110 millimeters (2.8 to 4.3 inches).

The Instituto Meteorológico Nacional forecast another 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) through Monday, with local peaks above 100 millimeters (3.9 inches) in the mountains. The damage followed quickly. Turrialba mayor Carlos Hidalgo Flores reported seven homes destroyed outright in his canton and others partially damaged, including one house flattened by a falling tree in Verbena Norte.

Red Cross crews pulled more than 160 people out of their homes across Sarapiquí and the Limón region, some by boat, many with pets and elderly relatives in tow. Roads took the worst of it. Route 32, the main link between San José and Limón, closed and reopened over the weekend. The bridge over the Río Chirripó on Route 4 in Sarapiquí stayed shut for close to 24 hours before inspectors cleared it Monday morning and found no structural damage.

By late morning, every road the rain had closed was open again. That is the recovery pattern worth understanding here, because it repeats: these routes shut fast, then reopen within a day once crews clear the material.

The other half of the country is running dry

Here is the part that makes this stretch genuinely unusual. While the Caribbean floods, the Pacific is in the middle of its driest spell of the year. A strong El Niño is in place, and forecasters expect it to hold through the rest of 2026, possibly strengthening further before it fades during 2027. El Niño tends to suppress rainfall on Costa Rica’s Pacific side and in the Central Valley while leaving the Caribbean wetter than normal.

Layered on top of that is the canícula, the mid-season dry spell that interrupts the Pacific rains in July and August. This year it arrived longer and more intense than usual. Fourteen weather stations set daily heat records on Aug. 11, the most in a single day so far this year, with Sardinal in Carrillo reaching 37.8 C (100 F). Every province recorded at least one except Limón.

So one strong El Niño is producing a flood emergency on one coast and a drought watch on the other, at the same time, in a country you can drive across in five hours.

What the next four weeks look like

The national outlook going from Aug. 17 through Sept. 13 keeps that split in place for a while yet. Through Aug. 23, the Caribbean stays wet, with weekly totals of 70 to 185 millimeters (2.8 to 7.3 inches) in the northern Caribbean and 35 to 95 millimeters (1.4 to 3.7 inches) in the south. The Northern Zone runs close to normal at 40 to 145 millimeters (1.6 to 5.7 inches). The entire Pacific stays very dry.

The following week, Aug. 24 to 30, looks much the same, with the canícula ending but El Niño keeping the central and northern Pacific in deficit. The turn comes around Aug. 31. From then through mid-September, the Caribbean and the Northern Zone are expected to settle back to normal levels for the season, while the Pacific, the Central Valley and the western Northern Zone stay dry.

Forecasters put the odds of another extreme event over the next two weeks at roughly 25% and do not currently expect a major system to strike directly in that window. That is a projection rather than a promise, and confidence drops sharply for the second week of September.

If you have travel booked this week

The Caribbean coast and the Northern Zone are the areas to watch. Puerto Viejo, Cahuita, Tortuguero, Sarapiquí, Guápiles and the Turrialba area have all seen road closures, river flooding or both in the last three days. Check road conditions before you set out, not after. Route 32 between San José and Limón and Route 4 through Sarapiquí are the two corridors most likely to shut on short notice, because both run below slopes that shed material once the ground is this wet.

Never drive into standing water on a flooded road. Half a meter (roughly 20 inches) of moving water is enough to float a vehicle, and you cannot see whether the road surface underneath is still there. If your plans are flexible, the Pacific is the obvious alternative right now. Guanacaste, the Nicoya Peninsula and the central Pacific are dry, sunny and running well below normal rainfall.

Call 911 if you need rescue or evacuation, and call early rather than waiting until water is at the door. The rain will ease. The open question is how fast the ground drains, because until saturation drops, every wave that crosses will land harder than the raw numbers suggest.

World.title: Fernández Tours Flooded Limón as Pressure Builds for an Emergency Declaration
World.content:
President Laura Fernández spent this morning touring flood-damaged communities in Limón province, as pressure built on her government to issue a formal emergency declaration for the Caribbean coast. Casa Presidencial released the itinerary last night and circulated an updated version at this morning

The schedule ran from a shelter visit in Valle La Estrella through damaged areas in Limón, Matina and Guácimo, closing at a shelter in Guácimo in the late afternoon, and included a meeting with agency heads and the mayor of Limón. Its been reported the tour was to begin at 8:45 a.m., while the agenda circulated Monday morning listed the first stop at 9:20 a.m.

The call for a declaration came yestarday afternoon from Mangell Mc Lean, a legislator with the opposition Partido Liberación Nacional who represents Limón. He said he had travelled through the province and described it as facing “a critical situation, with destroyed roads and isolated communities,” adding that he had contacted local authorities before formally asking the president to consider a declaration for the Costa Rican Caribbean.

Article 29 of the National Emergency and Risk Prevention Law, allows the executive branch to declare a state of emergency anywhere in the country by decree. This effect is financial since a declaration lifts the ordinary budget constraints imposed by Article 180 of the Constitution, which lets the government move money quickly and contract reconstruction work under an exception regime instead of standard public procurement timelines.

Once a decree is signed, the Comisión Nacional de Emergencias must produce a General Emergency Plan setting out the causes of the disaster, an estimate of damage and losses, and the works required to address it. Public institutions then have 30 days to submit documented damage reports, with a further 30 days available, and the commission verifies that the damage was actually caused by the event before any project enters the plan. The money runs through the National Emergency Fund.

The same stretch of coast has been through the process before. In 2021, an executive decree placed Limón, Matina, Pococí, Guácimo, Siquirres and Talamanca under a state of emergency, alongside Turrialba, Jiménez, Sarapiquí and five cantons in Alajuela, after a Caribbean storm system.

The damage that prompted Mc Lean’s request accumulated across the weekend as tropical wave No. 32 crossed. The Comisión Nacional de Emergencias reported 495 people in shelters nationwide as of its 5 p.m. Sunday count, distributed across 11 sites. Its earlier count, taken at 4:25 p.m. Sunday, logged 154 people sheltered in the Caribbean, with 11 at the Matina community hall, 67 at Escuela La Plástica in Valle La Estrella and 76 at Escuela Pandora Oeste. Reports have 134 people sheltered in Limón province.

The Costa Rican Red Cross evacuated 65 people across the Limón area, with 16 in Matina, 15 in Cariari de Pococí, 14 in Río Jiménez de Guácimo, 16 in Talamanca and four in Valle La Estrella. More than 100 others were evacuated in Sarapiquí. The Cuerpo de Bomberos reported responding to more than 33 flood incidents and rescuing roughly 150 people.

Rising flow on the Río Sixaola has left the communities of Gandoca and Sixaola without road access. In Turrialba, mayor Carlos Hidalgo Flores reported seven homes as total losses, among them a house destroyed by a falling tree in Verbena Norte, in the Santa Rosa district. The Ministerio de Educación Pública cancelled Monday classes across the Limón and Sulá regional directorates.

The commission, headed by Alejandro Picado, is holding an orange alert over the Northern Zone, the entire Caribbean slope and the canton of Turrialba, with a yellow alert across the Central Valley, Central Pacific and South Pacific. Only the North Pacific sits outside the alert system altogether.

The flooding is the first large natural disaster to test the Fernández administration, which took office on May 8 and holds 31 of the 57 seats in the Legislative Assembly. Whether it signs a declaration will determine how quickly damaged roads, bridges and drainage systems along the Caribbean are rebuilt, and how much of that work is paid for outside ordinary budget channels.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Corcovado Faces Ranger Shortage and Environmental Crime
World.content:
Concerns are growing over Costa Rica’s ability to protect Corcovado National Park as park rangers contend with illegal gold mining, poaching, logging, illegal fishing and incursions into protected land while working with limited personnel and resources. The latest warning comes from environmental advocates who say environmental crimes are increasing inside and around the park on the Osa Peninsula.

Bernardo Aguilar, president of the Civic Environmental Parliament, has called for more personnel dedicated to surveillance, protection and maintenance. The staffing numbers show the challenge. SINAC data released this summer indicated that Corcovado had 48 park rangers as of June 17.

But Enrique Obando, a ranger working in Corcovado, said only about 15 were assigned primarily to control and protection duties, while the others were needed for tourism and other park operations. He estimated that each protection ranger is effectively responsible for roughly 3,000 hectares of difficult tropical forest terrain.

Corcovado protects 42,570 hectares of land and another 5,375 hectares of marine territory. Its forests, beaches, wetlands and coastal waters provide habitat for some of Costa Rica’s best-known wildlife, including jaguars, tapirs, pumas and peccaries. The dangers facing those charged with protecting the park became particularly clear earlier this year.

Four men were detained in January after rangers discovered an alleged illegal gold-mining operation along the Sirena River. Investigators said the group had equipment including GPS devices, water pumps and a generator. One suspect escaped, while several of those detained allegedly threatened park rangers during the operation. The case is under investigation by environmental prosecutors.

Rangers have also encountered increasingly organized mining operations in remote parts of Corcovado. During another operation in March, eight rangers walked approximately 10 kilometers from the Los Patos station to reach an illegal mining camp. Three men were detained and mining equipment was seized. Rangers involved in the operation described working with limited communications and relying partly on outside conservation groups for food, equipment and other logistical support.

Illegal gold mining has long been a problem on the Osa Peninsula, but recent investigations have raised concerns that some operations are becoming better financed and equipped. Rangers have reported finding miners with metal detectors and satellite phones, making enforcement in Corcovado’s remote interior increasingly difficult. The staffing pressure extends beyond Corcovado.

A University of Costa Rica report published in June found that SINAC had 137 employees throughout the entire Osa Conservation Area, which includes Corcovado, Piedras Blancas and Marino Ballena national parks along with several other protected areas. The same report cited the 2025 State of the Nation report showing that SINAC’s overall budget had fallen by about 40% after several consecutive years of reductions.

The problem is not limited to land. Illegal fishing and removal of marine resources have also been identified as threats in areas associated with Corcovado, adding a large stretch of coastline and ocean to the territory authorities must monitor. For Costa Rica, the stakes extend beyond conservation.

Corcovado is one of our most important nature-tourism destinations and a centerpiece of tourism on the Osa Peninsula. Thousands of travelers visit the region each year specifically for its rainforest and wildlife, making effective protection of the park important both environmentally and economically.

Costa Rica has long promoted its national parks and protected areas as central to its international reputation. In Corcovado, however, rangers are being asked to protect a vast and difficult landscape while simultaneously managing visitors, responding to environmental crimes and confronting operations that can be increasingly organized and dangerous.

The latest warnings are renewing a familiar question: whether the resources assigned to protect one of Costa Rica’s most valuable wild areas are keeping pace with the threats inside it.

World.title: BREAKING: Tyrel Robinson reportedly shot and killed near Belize City bus terminal
World.content:
BREAKING: Tyrel Robinson reportedly shot and killed near Belize City bus terminal

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A man identified as Tyrel Robinson was reportedly shot and killed near the Belize City bus terminal on Monday evening.

The shooting reportedly occurred in the Martin’s area, near the terminal, shortly after 5:00 p.m.

Police responded to the scene following reports of gunfire, and Robinson was identified as the victim.

Details surrounding the circumstances of the shooting remain limited at this time, including the motive and whether police have identified any suspects.

Police investigations are ongoing.

World.title: Yellow Ginger Fest 2026 held in Punta Gorda
World.content:
Yellow Ginger Fest 2026 held in Punta Gorda

By Zoila Palma: On August 15, 2026, the annual Yellow Ginger Festival celebrated its 11th year with Park Fest 2026, held at Punta Gorda’s Central Park under the theme “Embrace Our Culture and Shape Our Future.”

The festival brought together members of the community to showcase the rich Indo-Belizean heritage of the East Indian community in southern Belize.

The event featured cultural performances, traditional cuisine and activities highlighting the customs and traditions passed down through generations.

Hon. Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture, President Vaughn and the NICH Board congratulated the Yellow Ginger Festival Committee for its continued dedication to safeguarding, promoting and celebrating East Indian traditions in Belize.

World.title: Two detained following early-morning shooting of San Pedro fisherman
World.content:
Two detained following early-morning shooting of San Pedro fisherman

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained two people in connection with the early-morning shooting of 26-year-old San Pedro fisherman John Hernandez, who was ambushed outside his residence on Sunday.

According to police, officers responded to the San Pedro Polyclinic at about 4:13 a.m. on August 16, where they found Hernandez suffering from gunshot injuries.

Investigators say Hernandez was entering his yard at around 3:50 a.m. when two men arrived outside his residence on a motorcycle. One of the men reportedly got off the motorcycle, ran toward Hernandez and fired several shots in his direction before fleeing.

Hernandez was initially taken to the San Pedro Polyclinic before being flown to Belize City for further treatment at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital. Police say he is now listed in stable condition.

The San Pedro Sun reported that Hernandez was wounded in the upper left shoulder and left leg and that several expended shell casings were recovered from the scene. The publication also reported an increased police presence and operations on the island following the shooting.

Hernandez is presently before the High Court in an unrelated case stemming from a July 31, 2024 incident in northern Ambergris Caye. He, Shelby Jonathan Hernandez and Hector Pop are jointly charged with one count of arson and two counts of aggravated assault after allegedly pursuing and firing at two fishermen before their boat was later set on fire. John Hernandez and Pop are presently out on bail, and the matter is scheduled to return to court on September 16 ahead of a trial expected in 2027.

Police have not announced a motive for Sunday morning’s shooting. Investigations continue.

World.title: IICA and Zamorano train Belizean dairy producers in sustainable production and processing
World.content:
IICA and Zamorano train Belizean dairy producers in sustainable production and processing

By Zoila Palma: The Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture (IICA) Delegation in Belize, in collaboration with Zamorano University in Honduras, hosted a five-day theoretical and practical workshop aimed at strengthening the capacity of Belizean milk producers and supporting a more sustainable and resilient dairy industry.

The workshop, held from August 11 to 15, 2026, was organized following a request for support from the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries. It brought together representatives from Belize’s northern and western dairy private sector, technical personnel from the Ministry’s Agroprocessing Unit and IICA Belize.

Participants received both classroom instruction and hands-on training in areas including sustainable milk production, livestock practices, forage management, feed use, milk quality and food safety, dairy microbiology and processing. The training also covered the production of cheese, yogurt and cream, quality control, cleaning and sanitation systems, and the sustainable use of whey and other dairy by-products.

The workshop also included technical visits to dairy facilities, where participants gained practical exposure to dairy cattle management, feed mills, calf facilities, milking parlors, laboratories and dairy processing operations.

IICA Belize said the initiative responds to “the need to build a more productive, competitive, sustainable and resilient dairy industry in Belize by equipping producers and technical personnel with practical tools to improve production, product quality and diversification”. IICA reaffirmed its commitment to working with national and regional partners to support Belize’s agriculture sector.

World.title: MoHW warns of increased Dengue risk during rainy season
World.content:
MoHW warns of increased Dengue risk during rainy season

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness (MoHW) is reminding Belizeans that the rainy season increases the risk of dengue transmission, as stagnant water provides breeding grounds for the Aedes aegypti mosquito.

The Ministry explained that dengue can cause mild to severe illness and, in some cases, can be fatal. Common symptoms include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, and skin rash, while severe cases may involve bleeding or difficulty breathing. Residents experiencing symptoms are urged to seek medical attention immediately.

The Ministry is encouraging residents to take steps around their homes, businesses and communities to eliminate mosquito breeding sites. These measures include emptying, covering or removing containers that collect water, disposing of discarded tires, bottles and cans, keeping drains and surroundings free of vegetation, garbage and debris, and using mosquito repellent as directed.

The Ministry said it continues to work with communities, local authorities and partners to strengthen dengue surveillance and vector control activities across the country. It emphasized that dengue prevention is a shared responsibility and urged residents to remain vigilant, particularly during the rainy season.

World.title: Minister of Education attends 2026 Taiwan Scholarship Orientation
World.content:
Minister of Education attends 2026 Taiwan Scholarship Orientation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Hon. Francis Fonseca, Minister of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, attended the 2026 Taiwan Scholarship Orientation along with H.E. Dame Froyla Tzalam, Governor-General of Belize, and H.E. Amino Chi, Ambassador of the Republic of China (Taiwan).

Minister Fonseca encouraged the scholarship recipients to capitalize on this valuable opportunity and serve as Belize’s ambassadors in Taiwan.

Fonseca also emphasized the importance of recipients returning home to Belize and putting into action what they learn through this opportunity.

Fonseca expressed appreciation to the Government and people of Taiwan for their “continued generosity and commitment to Belize’s development,” particularly through investments in education and opportunities for Belizean students.

World.title: Maclovio Ack emerges as PUP’s Punta Gorda mayoral candidate
World.content:
Maclovio Ack emerges as PUP’s Punta Gorda mayoral candidate

By Zoila Palma: On August 16, 2026, the People’s United Party (PUP) held its municipal convention in Punta Gorda Town (PG) to select its mayoral candidate and six councilor candidates for the 2027 Municipal Elections. The convention took place at the Toledo Community College from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

According to the PUP, 1,233 ballots were cast, with the party describing the turnout as the “largest municipal convention recorded in the history of PG.”

Following the close of polls and the counting of ballots, Maclovio Ack emerged victorious as the PUP’s mayoral candidate for the 2027 Municipal Elections in Punta Gorda Town.

The PUP also congratulated the six successful councilor candidates, namely Gloria Avila, Anthony Fuentes, Kerlin Moreira, Olivia Sho, Indira Coleman and Roberto Virez. Avila topped the polls among the councilor candidates.

The party also extended appreciation to the mayoral and councilor candidates who were unsuccessful at the PG convention, commending them for their participation and contribution to the party’s democratic process.

World.title: Hell Hath No Fury: Barefooted woman in black ransacks nail tech’s house; Stabs up couch, mattress, cuts up clothes and empties acetone, nail polish, BBQ sauce, soda over everything
World.content:
Hell Hath No Fury: Barefooted woman in black ransacks nail tech’s house; Stabs up couch, mattress, cuts up clothes and empties acetone, nail polish, BBQ sauce, soda over everything

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 45-year-old Belize City woman has been charged with burglary and aggravated assault following a bizarre incident in which a nail technician reported that her home and business equipment were extensively damaged, with furniture allegedly stabbed repeatedly and several items covered in sauces, cosmetics and other liquids.

Police say the 23-year-old homeowner reported that at around 7:49 p.m. on Friday, August 14, she was at a mechanic shop when she received a telephone call from a friend informing her that a woman dressed entirely in black and barefooted had been seen inside her home.

The woman immediately sought police assistance and returned to the residence with officers, where she allegedly discovered extensive damage.

According to the police report, two small sofas and a mattress had been stabbed approximately 25 times and smeared or soaked with substances including barbecue sauce, hair jam, nail polish, acetone, soap water, coconut oil and red Fanta.

Ten pillows had reportedly been ripped open, while a table used by the woman for her nail business was damaged with acetone and powder. Nail polish, nail buffers and cosmetic powders were also allegedly destroyed.

The woman additionally reported that a number of her clothing valued at approximately $2,500 had been cut and soaked with acetone, while several bottles of vitamins and tonic had been emptied.

A bottle of Chanel perfume valued at $290, a Samsung S7 cellphone and Social Security and bank cards were also reported missing. The woman estimated the total value of the damaged and missing property at approximately $6,007.

Police subsequently detained 45-year-old housekeeper Roumayne Veleen Andrews. On Sunday, August 16, Andrews was formally arrested and charged with burglary and aggravated assault.

World.title: 10 interesting facts on the birthday of Marcus Garvey
World.content:
Marcus Garvey

On the 139th anniversary of the birth of Marcus Garvey, Jamaica’s first national hero, Observer Online shares some interesting facts about the late Pan-Africanist.

Garvey was born in St Ann’s Bay, St Ann in 1887. His message of black empowerment is the driving force of the Pan African movement he started in 1920 while living in New York, where he was a pillar of the Harlem Renaissance.

His teachings inspired many freedom fighters across the globe including Dr Martin Luther King Jr and Malcolm X, and recording artistes like Bob Marley and Burning Spear.

He died in London in June 1940 at age 52. Here are some interesting facts below.

1. Garvey’s parents, Malcus Mosiah Garvey Snr, a stone mason, and Sarah Jane Richards, a domestic worker, had 11 children. However, only Marcus Garvey and his elder sister Indiana lived to adulthood, with the other nine siblings dying in early childhood.

2. Garvey attended elementary school in Jamaica until age 14, and was thereafter instructed privately by tutors. As a young man, he had a talent for public speaking.

3. As a teen, Garvey migrated from St Ann to Kingston, where he worked as a printer and became involved in politics and trade unionism, leading a major print workers’ strike in 1908.

4. He published the short-lived political magazine, “The Watchman”, inspired by George William Gordon’s historical abolitionist paper. It folded after three issues.

5. As Garvey travelled internationally, he observed the poor living conditions and victimization of black people, compelling him to empower people of African descent.

6. On Emancipation Day in 1914, in Jamaica, he launched the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA), encouraging self-government for black people worldwide; self-help economic projects and protest against racial discrimination.

7. The first UNIA division was formed in New York in May 1917, and within a month, it had two million members across the US. By 1920, there were 1,100 chapters in 40 countries around the world.

8. Garvey launched the UNIA’s Black Star Line Steamship Corporation in New York in 1919, aimed at establishing an efficient mode of transportation, communication and trade among black people globally while enhancing the image and pride of black people.

9. Garvey had numerous enemies, including FBI director J Edgar Hoover and fellow black leader W.E.B. Du Bois, who opposed Garvey’s separatism and repatriation efforts. Du Bois and NAACP members organised the ‘Garvey Must Go’ campaign to have the Jamaican deported.

10. Marcus Garvey was twice married. His and his first wife, Amy Ashwood Garvey, divorced after three years of marriage. He and second wife, Amy Jacques Garvey, had two sons – Marcus Garvey Jnr and Julius Winston Garvey.

World.title: Defend truth, liberty
World.content:
Reverend Astor Carlyle (right) shakes hands with Governor General Sir Patrick Allen as Lady Allen (second right) and Chief of Defence Staff Vice Admiral Antonette Wemyss Gorman (left) look on at the end of Sunday’s church service commemorating 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension, Up Park Camp in St Andrew. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Jamaicans have been urged to summon the courage of a previous generation and stand firm in defence of truth and liberty just as men and women from this region answered the call to serve when World War II plunged the world into geopolitical turmoil and economic uncertainty.



Reverend Captain Astor Carlyle made the appeal on Sunday in his sermon during the service celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Royal Air Forces Association (RAFA) Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension inside the Jamaica Defence Force’s Up Park Camp headquarters in St Andrew.

According to RAFA, the service, held under the theme ‘80 years of service, sacrifice, and unity’, marks the commencement of a year of celebrations to mark its founding.

Referencing the first lesson — Isaiah 6:1-8, which tells of the prophet Isaiah seeing a vision of God, realising he is sinful, gets cleansed by a burning coal, and volunteers to serve God by saying, ‘Here am I. Send me!’ — Rev Carlyle said that in the time of Isaiah, Judah needed someone to shoulder the responsibility of being God’s representative during great confusion.

“Throughout the Bible, God asks questions, but there is one question from the lips of God that is very relevant for a day like this when we celebrate 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association; it is a question that we heard in the first scripture reading today: Whom shall I send? Who will go for us? And this was a question asked of the prophet Isaiah in a time that needed a Godly voice and a Godly presence to bring calm and consciousness to a nation in crisis,” Carlyle told the congregation of mostly ex-servicemen and women.

“This was a time of chaos, a time of complexity, a time of corruption, and when the young Isaiah stood in the presence of God and considered the grave need, he responded with five words, ‘Here am I, send me.’ Isaiah saw what was at stake, and without concern for himself, he answered in the affirmative,” Carlyle said.

“This is a picture of the kind of spirit with which our Caribbean service members engaged the desperate call from the allied forces in 1939. It was a time of geopolitical and economic instability. Dictators were emerging in Europe and Asia, threatening the fragile peace that the Treaty of Versailles sought to ensure. The Great Depression and the subsequent invasion of Poland required the allied forces to sound the rallying call, and with a spirit of duty and a sense of mission our Caribbean servicemen said ‘Here am I, send me.’ Some trained as pilots, some trained as navigators, some were ground crew under the British Commonwealth air training plan.

“They served in Europe, they served in North Africa, they served in the Mediterranean, they served in Asia. Many Jamaicans served with the Royal Air Force bomber command and fighter command, defending Britain during air raids and helping push back the Axis forces. These young men of the Caribbean faced grave danger, but not for fame or reward, they believed in freedom that was worth defending and they paid the ultimate sacrifice. That is why we celebrate their gallantry today,” Carlyle said.

He stated that the service Jamaicans gave during the war stands as a reminder that the call to duty is for the willing, and encouraged citizens to demonstrate a willingness to serve, just as the war veterans did.

“Isaiah displayed that spirit when God asked ‘Whom shall I send?’ He didn’t give excuses, he didn’t say I am not qualified enough or I have too many responsibilities, or I am too young or I am too old. He simply said, ‘Here I am, send me.’ That is the heart of a willing servant. God expects the same of you and me, He’s asking us that same question today. As our world shows signs of economic shocks and geopolitical uncertainty God is asking who is willing, who will stand for truth, who will serve?” Carlyle told the congregation.

Earlier, in her welcome, RAFA President Major (Retired) Johanna Lewin shared that the founding members of the organisation, formed on August 16, 1946, were a band of merry men who served in the Royal Air Force during World Ward II and did so with a deep sense of pride.

RAFA, she said, initially was for those who served in the war and returned home to Jamaica “to continue their camaraderie and visit the proverbial river — the bar”.

“They wanted to ensure that all was not forgotten and that the comradeship and shared sense of duty that they developed during the war years were persevered. How many of you are familiar with Colonel Reggie Chin, who was commanding officer of the Third Battalion for many years and who served with RAF during the war? How many of you are familiar with Michael Manley, former [Jamaica] prime minister, who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force during World War II? We could be here all day. It’s a long story and cannot be given justice here,” Lewin said.

She shared that RAFA started under a hut at one end of the airfield at the JDF Air Wing in Up Park Camp.

“We were offered three prime camp locations, but the one selected was what we know as Curphey Place in Swallowfield, the home of RAFA and the Jamaica Legion. The land was eventually given in perpetuity for the benefit of veterans. RAFA evolved and became more than just a means for these sassy World War II veterans to visit the ever-present river and chat and reminisce and sing about their experiences in Britain,” Lewin said.

“One of the early and major philanthropic works took place when the British charity… established Cheshire Homes, what we would term a hospice. RAFA was the first local entity to pledge $10,000, a tidy sum in those days, to build one of the units. Cheshire Homes is what we now know as the Mona Rehab. We were able to fund the original columbarium in Briggs Park and now the extension. RAFA has continued its tradition of raising funds and giving,” Lewin said.

World.title: First hurdle cleared
World.content:
KOZYCKI... campaign focused on fighting corruption, working to rebuild trust in Government; tackling affordability, lowering the costs for working families; and expanding access to affordable and quality health care

NEW YORK, USA — The Georgia-based attorney who says he was inspired to run for a seat in the United States Congress to help deportees like Jamaican Godfrey Wade has cleared the first hurdle, winning the Democratic Party’s primary in the state’s 7th Congressional District.

Tony Kozycki, an immigration lawyer, said he was disgusted by the system when he represented Jamaican-born US veteran Godfrey Wade and discovered how difficult it was to get him his day in court for a repaid bounced cheque and an unproven assault charge 12 years ago.

Wade, who lived legally in the US for 50 years, served overseas in the military and was honourably discharged. After being flagged for the offences he was deported to Jamaica earlier this year. Kozycki has since been fighting the case, with little success. He never became a US citizen.

Asked for an update on the case, the attorney told the Jamaica Observer, which carried the deportation story, that there had not been any major new legal developments or petitions filed on Wade’s behalf.

“However, we have not given up, as I still believe Godfrey deserves the opportunity to return to the United States and have his case heard fairly. We continue to advocate for him and remain committed to seeing him receive the process he deserves,” said Kozycki.

“Wade’s case did more than expose a broken immigration system, it exposed a failure of representation by Rich McCormick,” Kozycki added.

McCormick is the Republican attorney, an incumbent whom Kozycki will face in the midterm elections for the Georgia 7th Congressional District, after snagging the Democratic Party nomination by polling 19,742 or 40 per cent of the votes against nearest rival Case Norton’s 11,036 or 22.3 per cent.

The other two contestants polled a combined 36,000 votes in the May 2026 primary. Kozycki returned to defeat filmmaker Norton in the run-off, after garnering 11,667 to Norton’s 5,561 votes.

Kozycki accused McCormick of failing to provide adequate representation for Wade.

Both he and Wade have consistently maintained that notices for the Jamaican to attend a hearing were never received, due to problems with an address used by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which they say courts records show.

Moreover, restitution of the bounced cheque and all applicable fees were made in full, according to Wade’s family. His attorney noted that no physical violence was ever alleged in the assault charge.

“All we are asking is for the case to be reopened and Mr Wade to have his day in court. There is no need to trust me or Godfrey, just look at the documents and the evidence. All we want is one day before a judge and I know we will win this case,” Kozycki told the Observer during an interview in March this year.

As for his campaign priorities, Kozycki said they centre on three issues: “Fighting corruption and working to rebuild trust in Government, tackling affordability and lowering the costs for working families, and expanding access to affordable and quality health care.”
