World.title: Former Alan Jones colleague tells court of currying favour through texts
World.content:
A man accusing Alan Jones of indecently assaulting him when the pair worked together has told a trial he instigated flirtatious messages about being a bachelor to the veteran broadcaster because he "knew he would like to be spoken to that way".

Complainant C has alleged he was indecently assaulted by the former radio host on eight separate occasions while working with Mr Jones in 2008.

The man told the trial last week that Mr Jones kissed him without consent several times in the lift of his Circular Quay apartment and at work, and touched his crotch in the car while he was driving the radio host, when he was aged in his early 20s.

The man also alleges another colleague witnessed Mr Jones grope his penis on the outside of his pants when the radio host asked him to sit next to him at a lunch in Mosman.

Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching relating to six male complainants between 2003 and 2020.

The trial continues. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Texts under scrutiny in court

Under cross-examination for a second day, Complainant C was asked about comments he previously made about working with Mr Jones including saying that staff were treated like "family" and that he had a "great time".

Complainant C said the comments were not a true representation of his time working with Mr Jones and told the trial he said them before he ever spoke to anyone about the allegations.

The complainant previously told the court he felt "anxious and uncomfortable" when he accompanied a politician, who he worked for at the time, for a meeting with Mr Jones at the broadcaster's Circular Quay apartment in 2015.

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC suggested his description of how he felt was untrue, telling the court that after the meeting, Complainant C responded to a message from Mr Jones saying: "was so lovely seeing you too. Haven't been this happy with work in a long time … made only better by seeing you today."

"That message was in response to a message from Alan saying, 'I look happy … how big is the c***, love my angel'," Complainant C said.

" I never would have told Alan that I was anxious or uncomfortable, I never would have been able to have written that to him. "

The complainant accepted that he instigated a range of text message exchanges with Mr Jones throughout 2015 including one saying, "listening to your voice at work, missing you … lots of love always P.S I'm a bachelor again", followed by a comment, which the complainant agreed was a reference to his own penis.

"Do you agree that this was a message that was part of regular banter?" Ms Bashir asked. "I did send that message because I knew that he would like it … that was a reference to how he liked to describe my penis," Complainant C said. "You were intending to titillate him [Mr Jones]?" Ms Bashir suggested. "I wouldn't use that word, but I certainly thought it was a way of carrying [sic] favour with him," Complainant C replied.

Gabrielle Bashir has been cross-examining Complainant C. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

The trial heard Mr Jones requested Complainant C drive him home from work when the two worked in the same office several years after the alleged indecent assaults occurred.

Ms Bashir asked why the complainant did not make an excuse as to why he could not drive Mr Jones and suggested he did not need to agree to the request.

"He didn't have a gun to my head, but I didn't want to say no, I didn't want to say no to Alan Jones," the complainant said.

Complainant C said there was no inappropriate behaviour during the car ride.

'Groomed for 10 years'

The court heard Mr Jones sent him a message when he arrived home saying, "wanted to hug you but not allowed for a soon to be married man" followed by "but what about the massive weapon do I just have to imagine".

The trial heard the complainant replied saying, "I loved spending time with you today … unexpected … would love to have hugged too … those Book of Mormon blokes have nothing on me".

The complainant accepted that he instigated a range of text message exchanges with Mr Jones. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

The complainant said the Book of Mormon comment was a reference to something Mr Jones had said in the car about actors in the play, who are from Africa, having "massive penises".

Complainant C accepted that he had also sent Mr Jones a winking face and eggplant emoji, which he said was in reference to his penis.

The complainant agreed that he sent those messages as an adult but said they were "consistent" with someone "who had been groomed for 10 years".

Ms Bashir put to Complainant C on at least 16 different occasions that the alleged assaults never occurred, which he rejected each time.

The complainant repeatedly said he "hates" reading the old messages he had sent but denied Ms Bashir's suggestion that he hated them because they "expose the fabrication" of his allegations.

The court heard Complainant C invited Mr Jones to his wedding despite feeling "reluctant" to do so and accepted a $2,000 wedding gift from the broadcaster.

The complainant rejected suggestions that his various messages thanking Mr Jones for the gift — including saying, "for you to be there by my side on a most special day means more than you realise" — were inconsistent with messages to their alleged abuser.

The trial before Judge Glenn Walsh continues.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Swans players face suspension as AFL set to lay charges; Labor signs off on gambling reform deal with Coalition
World.content:
Key Sydney players are set to be charged by the AFL with bringing the game into disrepute and face suspension for multiple matches.

Two senior competition sources speaking on the condition of anonymity have confirmed to this masthead that the AFL will enact rule 2.3A, which prohibits conduct unbecoming or likely to prejudice the interests or reputation of the AFL, after the players returned to the team hotel in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning following a night of drinking.

The Sydney Swans logo.

The league’s action is separate to the Victoria Police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman in East Melbourne.

If the players are found to have broken an AFL rule, they can expect to be suspended for at least two matches, which would be unrelated to the police investigation.

World.title: Cricket star David Warner tried to switch seats before random breath test
World.content:
NationalCourts Cricket star David Warner tried to switch seats before random breath test Tom Wark August 18, 2026 — 2:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian cricket star David Warner has lamented global media attention about his drink-driving offence, suggesting it cost him valuable overseas commercial opportunities. The 39-year-old was convicted and fined $1500 on Tuesday for mid-range drink-driving after he tried to switch seats with a passenger when approaching a random breath-testing site in Sydney’s east on Easter Sunday. Former Australian Test cricketer David Warner leaves Waverley Local Court on Tuesday. AAPIMAGE The star batter’s barrister argued he should be spared conviction for the offence – when he blew more than twice the legal limit – because he had suffered extra punishment as a result of media coverage. Awais Ahmad told Waverley Local Court his client’s indiscretion had been covered in global outlets including ESPN, Al Jazeera and the Indian Express.



Countries including India and Bangladesh, where Warner might be seeking to play in T20 franchise leagues, have an acceptance of a “non-drinking culture”, Ahmad said. “The consequences of his offending are profound,” Ahmad said. Warner in action for the Sydney Thunder in 2025. Getty Images “Commercial opportunities (are) being affected.” Warner was arrested while he was on an Easter trip home from the subcontinent, where he captained the Karachi Kings in the Pakistan Super League.



When Warner saw the breath-testing site, he stopped short and attempted to swap seats with a female passenger, the agreed facts read out in court state. Once police identified him as the driver, he co-operated with the testing, Judge Clare Farnan noted. Ahmad questioned the decision of NSW Police to issue a press release about Warner’s arrest given the unremarkable nature of the offence. “The media onslaught thereafter has been quite profound,” the lawyer said. Farnan said there was evidence of cruel social media commentary directed at Warner and his wife Candice Warner.



Related Article Courts Cricket star David Warner pleads guilty to drink-driving His position as captain of the Sydney Thunder in the domestic Big Bash League was also under threat, the cricketer’s lawyer said. The Thunder, along with rival Sydney Sixers and Sheffield Shield team the NSW Blues, are part of a state government campaign to deter drink-driving. Despite the star batter’s pleas, Farnan said the need to deter the public from drink-driving was paramount in her decision to convict him. More than 17,300 people had come before the court in the past five years for mid-range drink-driving, she said.



“I accept Mr Warner is unlikely to reoffend,” she said. “(But) regrettably, drink-driving is still a significant factor in many crashes in NSW.” The offence was aggravated because children were in the car at the time, the judge said. Warner will be able to drive after he applies for an interlock licence and has the device fitted to his car. The interlock will prevent the car from starting if it detects alcohol in his system.

Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Swans players set to be charged under AFL rules as police investigation continues Sam McClure August 18, 2026 — 1:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key Sydney players are set to be charged by the AFL with bringing the game into disrepute and face suspension for multiple matches. Two senior competition sources speaking on the condition of anonymity have confirmed to this masthead that the AFL will enact rule 2.3A, which prohibits conduct unbecoming or likely to prejudice the interests or reputation of the AFL, after the players returned to the team hotel in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning following a night of drinking. Clockwise from left: Swans players Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard The league’s action is separate to the Victoria Police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman in East Melbourne. If the players are found to have broken an AFL rule, they can expect to be suspended for at least two matches, which would be unrelated to the police investigation.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation The Swans and the AFL are expected to make a joint announcement in relation to the league’s response to the alleged incident, according to the sources, which could be as early as Tuesday but is more likely to be announced on Wednesday. This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and one other player after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. World.content:
Breaking SportCricketAustralian cricket Weatherald axed as selectors send SOS to Renshaw Daniel Brettig Updated August 18, 2026 — 1:00pm ,first published 12:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cairns: Jake Weatherald has been dropped from the Australian team and fellow opener Matt Renshaw called up after their heavy loss to Bangladesh in the first Test in Darwin. Weatherald made two low scores at Marrara Stadium and looked uneasy at the batting crease, having admitted that his fate would be out of his hands if he didn’t make a score in his hometown. Matthew Renshaw has been recalled by the Australian selectors. Getty Images The brutality of the call was enhanced by the selectors’ decision not even to take Weatherald on to Mackay as part of the squad, a decision that may also rule him out of the Test tour of South Africa in October. “You are required to make runs all the time when you’re out there, and I’ve got a good opportunity to play two games hopefully and make some runs,” Weatherald had said. “If I don’t do that, then yeah I put my fate in someone else’s hands and I haven’t done enough.



"It's a challenge when people you respect say things about your batting, or your game. You're naturally always looking for affirmation, and people to respect what you're doing, but at the same time it's a part of cricket. “I understand now it’s just a part of the game I’m playing, but it’s a great challenge as well. That’s what makes Test cricket so hard, you’re in the spotlight, you need to do a lot of things, not just make runs. If you can do it all, it makes for a good career.” Loading Renshaw made his Test debut as a 20-year-old a decade ago and was harshly left out of the team the following year when he was replaced by Cameron Bancroft. Ironically, Renshaw’s last Tests in that initial stint with the team were in Australia’s previous series against Bangladesh in 2017. He has made sporadic appearances since while honing his game but in recent times has been a consistent presence in white ball squads and was the best performing batter on the recent limited overs tour of Bangladesh where the hosts best Australia in the ODI series.



More recently, Renshaw was part of the extended 19-man training squad in Brisbane ahead of the Darwin Test. Skipper Pat Cummins had alluded to the likelihood of a batting change after the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh. "I think it's a balance of it's one Test, but it's also a bit of a trend as well, so trying to work out do you need to intervene now, or let it play out, and you think it's the way forward," Cummins said. Jake Weatherald has lost his spot in the Test team Getty Images “That’s the question over the next couple of days, we’ll sit down and have a think, selectors will have a think, is there something there that’s going to take us forward, or is it starting to become a trend that we think needs to be changed. “It’s pretty clear it’s not quite functioning as well as we’d like as a group, so I’m sure the batters will get together and talk. Review some footage, review methods, their approaches to how they were this week. If we need to make some changes to our style, we’ve got a week or so and we better do it pretty quickly.”



Former Test opener and fellow Queenslander Matthew Hayden has been an outspoken advocate for Renshaw’s return to Test cricket at the top of the order. Related Article Australian cricket ‘He needs big runs’: Blowtorch on Marnus as selectors hear growing calls for change “I want some experience at the top,” Hayden said on Seven. “I want to see Matt Renshaw and I’ve been saying this for at least 12 months. I think he is match fit … I think the selectors knew what he was, now I want to see what he actually is.” More to come News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Cricket star David Warner tried to switch seats before random breath test
World.content:
NationalCourts Cricket star David Warner tried to switch seats before random breath test Tom Wark August 18, 2026 — 2:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian cricket star David Warner has lamented global media attention about his drink-driving offence, suggesting it cost him valuable overseas commercial opportunities. The 39-year-old was convicted and fined $1500 on Tuesday for mid-range drink-driving after he tried to switch seats with a passenger when approaching a random breath-testing site in Sydney’s east on Easter Sunday. Former Australian Test cricketer David Warner leaves Waverley Local Court on Tuesday. AAPIMAGE The star batter’s barrister argued he should be spared conviction for the offence – when he blew more than twice the legal limit – because he had suffered extra punishment as a result of media coverage. Awais Ahmad told Waverley Local Court his client’s indiscretion had been covered in global outlets including ESPN, Al Jazeera and the Indian Express.



Countries including India and Bangladesh, where Warner might be seeking to play in T20 franchise leagues, have an acceptance of a “non-drinking culture”, Ahmad said. “The consequences of his offending are profound,” Ahmad said. Warner in action for the Sydney Thunder in 2025. Getty Images “Commercial opportunities (are) being affected.” Warner was arrested while he was on an Easter trip home from the subcontinent, where he captained the Karachi Kings in the Pakistan Super League.



When Warner saw the breath-testing site, he stopped short and attempted to swap seats with a female passenger, the agreed facts read out in court state. Once police identified him as the driver, he co-operated with the testing, Judge Clare Farnan noted. Ahmad questioned the decision of NSW Police to issue a press release about Warner’s arrest given the unremarkable nature of the offence. “The media onslaught thereafter has been quite profound,” the lawyer said. Farnan said there was evidence of cruel social media commentary directed at Warner and his wife Candice Warner.



Related Article Courts Cricket star David Warner pleads guilty to drink-driving His position as captain of the Sydney Thunder in the domestic Big Bash League was also under threat, the cricketer’s lawyer said. The Thunder, along with rival Sydney Sixers and Sheffield Shield team the NSW Blues, are part of a state government campaign to deter drink-driving. Despite the star batter’s pleas, Farnan said the need to deter the public from drink-driving was paramount in her decision to convict him. More than 17,300 people had come before the court in the past five years for mid-range drink-driving, she said.



“I accept Mr Warner is unlikely to reoffend,” she said. “(But) regrettably, drink-driving is still a significant factor in many crashes in NSW.” The offence was aggravated because children were in the car at the time, the judge said. Warner will be able to drive after he applies for an interlock licence and has the device fitted to his car. The interlock will prevent the car from starting if it detects alcohol in his system.
